records.people: National Bank of Moldova management and Executive Committee (unnamed); Supervisory Board
records.summary: The Court of Accounts of the Republic of Moldova, by Decision no. 62 of 5 November 2019, published in the Monitorul Oficial on 29 November 2019, reported on a compliance audit of the National Bank of Moldova's administrative expenditure budgets and investment allocations for 2015 to 2018. It found non-compliance by responsible persons with certain provisions, performance bonuses paid without any regulation of incentive conditions, assets placed in inappropriate depreciation categories creating uncertainty over 4.1 million lei of book value, and concert organisation services worth 0.87 million lei procured with deficiencies relative to the regulatory framework with a possible impact on public revenues. This record rests on a specialist accounting-news report of the decision rather than on the Court's own published text, which could not be retrieved here.
records.detail: This is a separate episode from the 2012-2016 banking-fraud investigation already on the map: different years, a different subject matter (the bank's own administrative spending and procurement), a different investigating body (the supreme audit institution rather than prosecutors), and no named individuals. The audit was reported as concluding that expenditure was executed in line with the regulatory framework in all material respects while identifying the uncertain situations listed above. The report was directed to the National Bank of Moldova, the Ministry of Finance, the Government and Parliament.
records.source_title: Curtea de Conturi: auditul devizelor de cheltuieli si a alocatiilor pentru investitii ale BNM

records.people: Czech National Bank as audited entity (no individuals named)
records.summary: The Supreme Audit Office (Nejvyssi kontrolni urad) audited the Czech National Bank's spending on asset acquisition and on operations for 2002 to 2004 under audit action 04/35, and its senate approved the audit conclusion on 10 October 2005. The conclusion records that the bank breached the Accounting Act, Act no. 563/1991 Sb., by treating some technical improvements to assets as operating expenditure, with errors totalling 592 thousand koruna; that uneconomical spending was found in payments for staff meals at certain training events, in payments of external partners' travel costs and in the limits set for domestic travel subsistence; that the bank failed to comply with the Accounting Act when carrying out its stocktake; that a 705 square metre plot of land in Prague was held neither on an inventory card nor in the accounting records, contrary to accounting rules; that artworks insured for 988,000 koruna were neither inventoried nor recorded off balance sheet; and that three flats let in Usti nad Labem were rented at least 50 per cent below average local market returns.
records.detail: The audit was carried out from November 2004 to May 2005 at the bank's head office and at its Ceske Budejovice, Usti nad Labem, Hradec Kralove and Brno branches. The bank objected to the audit protocol and appealed the decision on its objections, both of which were disposed of before the conclusion was approved. The conclusion also records that the bank's budget in the audited period did not include all expenditure or planned income, and notes that the Supreme Audit Office's remit over the bank is confined by statute to asset-acquisition and operating expenditure. This is a wholly separate episode from the 2026 embezzlement investigation already on the map: different decade, different conduct and a different body making the finding.
records.source_title: Kontrolni zaver 04/35 - Vydaje na porizeni majetku a na provoz Ceske narodni banky, Vestnik NKU 2005, castka 4, s. 421

blanks.document_and_section: KLSH (Kontrolli i Larte i Shtetit), Buletini Vjetor 2025 (klsh.org.al, 35 MB PDF, 457,074 characters of extracted text, grepped in full), plus KLSH's own final report 'Mbi Auditimin e Ushtruar ne 23 Subjekte Auditimi' for 2014 (approved by Chairman's Decision no. 17 of 28 February 2015), read in full.
blanks.what_it_said: Neither document records any KLSH audit of the Bank of Albania as an audited entity. The annual bulletin's only mention of the bank is a TAIEX workshop at which Dutch central-bank advisers and KLSH discussed 'roli dhe fusheveprimi i auditimeve te KLSH-se mbi Banken e Shqiperise ne situaten aktuale' - the role and scope of such audits in the present situation and under Albania's future EU obligations - which is a discussion about the scope of the vein, not an audit. The 23-subject report's three mentions of the bank are recommendations addressed to the Ministry of Finance: A/12 asks for better coordination with monetary policy because Ministry borrowing from the Bank of Albania exceeds short-term limits, and two further passages note that the bank itself, with the IMF, drafted legal proposals. The Ministry is the audited subject there, not the bank, and a recommendation is not a finding against the bank. The supreme-audit-institution vein is closed for Albania at these documents; other routes are untested.

blanks.what_it_said: The Audit Office of BiH Institutions delivered financial audit reports on 72 BiH institutions for 2022, described throughout as '72 budzetska korisnika' - 72 budget users. The word 'banka' does not occur anywhere in the document, and the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina is not among the audited bodies the Audit Office reported to Parliament. This is the inversion test described in the brief and it fails for Bosnia: the state audit institution's remit runs to budget users and the self-financing central bank is outside it. No second BiH episode was sought by any other route this round.

Both filed records were checked against have_cases.json and have_events.json for their country on the person, the episode and the source URL. Moldova's existing case is the 2012-2016 bank-fraud investigation of Dragutanu and three others, and its three existing events are two 2015 resignations under pressure and the Armasu dismissal: no overlap with a 2019 compliance audit of administrative spending. Czechia's existing case is a 2026 embezzlement investigation of unnamed staff sourced to Central Banking, and its existing event is Zeman's 2015 public pressure over board appointments: no overlap with a 2005 NKU audit conclusion on 2002-2004 spending.

party_names.json was grepped for audit-institution spellings before writing. It carries no name for the Czech Supreme Audit Office or the Moldovan Court of Accounts, so no existing spelling was available to match; the institutions are named in the summaries only, as these are case records and carry no entity field. The map's nearest existing forms are 'State Audit Office of the Republic of Macedonia' and 'State Audit Office of Hungary', and the new names were written in the same plain English style.

The Moldova record is filed with weak_source true and says so in its own summary, because the source is a specialist accounting-news portal reporting the Court of Accounts decision rather than the Court's own published text. Its quote field is deliberately omitted: the Romanian fragments I have came back inside a fetch summary rather than from my own copy and paste, so under this round's rule they were not trusted.
The Czechia quote was copied from the pdftotext output of the NKU PDF itself and is character-for-character the document's words.
Status strings: both records are filed as 'official finding', which is accurate - a supreme audit institution's approved audit conclusion. No status outside the closed list was needed.
